title: Towards a Theory of Robot Intelligence
content: Note: Work in progress. I have been having these late night thoughts on what could be an interesting theory of robot intelligence. For context, I’m a young roboticist, I’ve been in the field for 2 years, and I’m just breaking into research. I’ve worked on all sides of robotics at the fundamental level - planning for manipulation and navigation, SLAM, visual perception, controls. I’ve not worked heavily on whole-body control, locomotion, etc. but I think those challenges are more inherently control-theoretic rather than planning. I’m not an expert, this article is probably just to segment my current thought process on what my observations (perception) is about regarding robotics. title: CoRL 2026, Day 1: absorbing the frontier model
content: Part of a three-day series. Start with the cross-day synthesis for background and definitions of the terms used here. Day 1 opened in the shadow of GPT-6 Astra, a general-purpose frontier model released two months earlier. It was not designed for robots, yet when connected directly to simulated robots it completed far more tasks than purpose-built robot foundation models. The day’s talks kept returning to one question: if a general model can already plan and act, what is left for robot learning? The answers clustered around three ideas. Physical control runs against a clock that slow models cannot meet. Contact and force are still poorly handled. And the benchmarks the field uses to measure progress can hide the failures that...

title: CoRL 2026, Day 2: from demonstrations to deployments
content: Part of a three-day series. See the cross-day synthesis for background and definitions. Day 1 established that general frontier models now handle much of a robot’s high-level reasoning. Day 2 turned to a more practical question: how do robot models become reliable enough to do real work? A generalist model that succeeds 80% of the time is impressive in a lab demo, but useless on a factory line that cannot stop. The day’s research sessions covered the tools for closing that gap: human video as training data, reinforcement learning after pretraining, force and touch, and humanoid control. The afternoon added production metrics from robots doing work in real factories. Human video as primary training data Collecting robot demonstrations by teleoperation...

title: CoRL 2026, Day 3: agents, world models, and the big debate
content: Part of a three-day series. See the cross-day synthesis for background and definitions. The last day had two halves with very different characters. The morning consisted of short research presentations: less opinion, more evidence about where current methods work and where they break. The afternoon moved to a concert hall for the conference’s set pieces: a keynote by Fei-Fei Li on world models, a conversation between Li and AMD’s chief executive Lisa Su, and a formal debate on the question underlying the whole week. Is today’s dominant recipe, imitating human demonstrations and then fine-tuning, enough to produce general-purpose robots that companies can sell at a profit? title: CoRL 2026: where robot learning thinks it is going
content: Per-day notes: Day 1 · Day 2 · Day 3 The Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) is the main venue where machine-learning methods for robots are presented. The 2026 edition, held in Austin in November, was the largest so far. Attendance roughly doubled to about 4,800 people, submissions tripled to about 2,100 papers, and around 40% of attendees came from industry. This note pulls together what the three days of talks, keynotes, and the closing debate suggest about where the field is heading. It focuses on three questions: what researchers now treat as solved, what they treat as open, and where academic and industrial views differ. title: CS231n — Lecture 1: History of computer vision
content: Course meta Stanford CS231n — Deep Learning for Computer Vision. Reading-along the 2024 lecture set. I’ll keep one note per lecture, plus separate notes for assignments. Lecture 1 — visual recognition through the years Biological roots Hubel & Wiesel (1959) — single-cell recordings in cat V1. Found simple cells responding to oriented edges, complex cells pooling over position. Inspired the hierarchical structure later baked into CNNs. Pre-deep era Block world (Roberts, 1963) — first attempt at 3D recovery. Generalized cylinders / pictorial structures — parts + springs. SIFT (Lowe, 1999) — keypoint matching that actually worked. HoG + linear SVM (Dalal & Triggs, 2005) — pedestrian detection. PASCAL VOC & later ImageNet drove benchmark culture. Deep era AlexNet (Krizhevsky 2012)...
